Americans are concerned about inflation.

Only 8% of US consumers expect their income to grow faster than inflation over the next year, the lowest proportion in at least 2 years.

This figure has declined -10 percentage points since November 2024.

At the same time, 20% anticipate their income to grow at roughly the same pace as inflation, near the lowest proportion since at least July 2024.

This means 72% of consumers expect inflation to outpace their income over the next year, the highest reading in at least 2 years.

By comparison, this figure stood at 58% in November 2024.

Americans are extremely pessimistic about their real purchasing power.

Everyone is positioned for rate cuts. The economy did not get the memo.

Atlanta Fed GDPNow is tracking 4.3% growth this quarter, and a new tailwind just joined AI capex and the tax bill: tariff refunds. The Treasury is handing duties back to companies, a fiscal boost worth about 0.2 point of GDP that lands straight in corporate earnings. July payrolls looked soft, but strip out the school-calendar seasonals and the World Cup rolling off and underlying job growth was near 70k, with jobless claims still around 200k.

Growth is running hotter than the market believes. That keeps the Fed parked and rates higher for longer, and it is long-duration bonds that keep paying the bill.

The AI data center boom has a home address, and it is Texas.

Texas has roughly 100 GW of planned data center capacity, more than Virginia and Utah, the next two states, combined. Virginia built the last era and still leads on what is running today at 17 GW. The next era is being poured in Texas.

For scale, 100 GW is more than the entire Texas grid has ever pulled at peak. ERCOT is already buried in interconnection requests and has started hitting pause. Every one of those centers needs power that does not exist yet. The real Texas AI trade is whoever builds the electrons: generation, gas, and the grid.

The Fed spent 15 years trying to make markets safer. It built a $2.4 trillion time bomb instead.

Hedge funds now hold $2.4 trillion of US Treasurys, up from $600 billion a decade ago, levered as much as 100 to 1. Every time the Fed backstops the market to kill risk, it invites more borrowing. That trade has already detonated twice, in 2020 and again in 2025.

Here is the loop. A rescue kills risk, cheap risk breeds leverage, the leverage breaks, and the next rescue prints even more money. The leftover QE money is what lit the last inflation. We are deep into the leverage phase now, and the Treasury market under your entire portfolio is the fuse.

South Korea's stock market is now more volatile than Bitcoin.

The KOSPI's return volatility hit 63% this year, above Bitcoin's 48% and nearly double Japan's. Two chip stocks, Samsung and SK Hynix, make up more than half the index. Retail traders piled into 2x leveraged ETFs, whose assets jumped from $5 billion to over $40 billion. The exchange tripped its circuit breaker nine times this year, versus once in all of 2024.

For decades, New York and London set the tone in Asia's markets. That era is ending.

From 2018 to 2025, funds based in nine Asian markets poured $635 billion into their own stocks. The 2022 to 2025 wave alone ran 7x the prior four years, while foreign inflows collapsed 81% to $26 billion. India passed the UK and France to become the world's 5th largest stock market.

Asian equities now have a homegrown buyer that does not bolt at the first crisis. The old trade of foreigners sell, Asia craters is breaking. The new risk lives inside: when locals crowd the same names, everyone leaves through one door.

📉 The Chinese 10-year sovereign yield has fallen back to around 1.68%, its lowest level since the summer of 2025, just as Beijing is about to release a key batch of economic data.

🇨🇳 When investors aggressively buy Chinese government bonds, they are generally expressing expectations of weak nominal growth, subdued inflation and a persistently accommodative monetary policy. This fits quite well with the broader picture as we have weak PMIs, investment under pressure, a still-depressed property sector and, above all, very soft credit demand.

⚠️ The upcoming data could matter for the policy response. At the end of July, Beijing still chose not to launch a major new stimulus package, preferring to let previously announced measures work through the economy. However, if the next data once again show weak consumption, disappointing investment, continued property weakness and a meaningful slowdown in industrial production, then the diagnosis becomes more serious as the weakness would no longer be concentrated in a few areas but would be spreading across domestic demand more broadly.

➡️ The change in the release time, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., obviously attracts attention, and what is worth watching is the broader timing. 

If those figures confirm the slowdown, they could become one of the final pieces of evidence pushing Beijing from measured support toward something more significant.

*Bloomberg link 1: https://t.co/Q9k50c6CAn
*Bloomberg link 2: https://t.co/g97LpZStTz
